Punctuation.question: Select the correctly punctuated letter complimentary close:
Punctuation.explanation: "Yours" is a possessive pronoun without apostrophe, followed by a comma.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Which sentence avoids a comma splice?

options.A: She studied hard; consequently, she topped the board.
options.B: She studied hard, consequently she topped the board.
options.C: She studied hard, she topped the board.
options.D: She studied hard consequently, she topped.

Punctuation.explanation: Avoids joining two independent clauses with just a comma (comma splice).

Punctuation.question: Identify the correct possessive form for "James":
Punctuation.explanation: Proper nouns ending in -s can take either 's or just an apostrophe.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Select the sentence with correct quotation punctuation:

options.A: "I will attend," she said, "if the weather permits."
options.B: "I will attend", she said, "if the weather permits".
options.C: "I will attend" she said, "if the weather permits."
options.D: "I will attend," she said "if the weather permits."

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Which punctuation mark represents the longest pause in spoken delivery?
Punctuation.explanation: The full stop represents the most complete grammatical and phonetic pause.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Which punctuation mark represents the shortest pause?
Punctuation.explanation: The comma indicates the briefest structural pause in reading.

Punctuation.question: Select the correct use of hyphens in numbers:
Punctuation.explanation: Compound numbers between 21 and 99 are hyphenated.

Punctuation.question: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?

options.A: Yes, I am ready to begin the examination.
options.B: Yes I am ready, to begin the examination.
options.C: Yes, I am ready, to begin, the examination.
options.D: Yes I am, ready to begin the examination.

Punctuation.explanation: Introductory conversational particle "Yes" is set off by a comma.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Identify the sentence with correct dialogue punctuation:

options.D: Ali exclaimed, What an outstanding performance!

Punctuation.explanation: Speaker tag is followed by comma, quote begins with capital, exclamation mark inside.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Which sentence correctly uses apostrophe for omission?
Punctuation.explanation: "o'clock" is a historical contraction of "of the clock".

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Select the correctly punctuated coordinate adjectives:

options.A: It was a cold, rainy, depressing afternoon.
options.B: It was a cold rainy depressing afternoon.
options.C: It was a cold, rainy, depressing, afternoon.
options.D: It was a cold; rainy; depressing afternoon.

Punctuation.explanation: Coordinate adjectives modifying the same noun are separated by commas.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Select the correctly punctuated complex sentence:

options.A: When the bell rang, the students left the classroom quietly.
options.B: When the bell rang the students left the classroom quietly.
options.C: When the bell, rang, the students left the classroom.
options.D: When the bell rang, the students, left the classroom.

Punctuation.explanation: Introductory subordinate clause takes a comma before main clause.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Identify the sentence with correct apostrophe usage for plural possession:

options.A: The boys' hostel is located near the university campus.
options.B: The boy's hostel is located near the university campus.
options.C: The boys hostel's is located near the university campus.
options.D: The boyes' hostel is located near the university campus.

Punctuation.explanation: For regular plural nouns ending in -s (boys), possession is shown by adding only an apostrophe at the end (boys').

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Choose the sentence with correct use of the semicolon:

options.A: The library was quiet; everyone was immersed in their books.
options.B: The library was quiet; and everyone was immersed in their books.
options.C: The library; was quiet everyone was reading.
options.D: The library was quiet, everyone was immersed in books;

Punctuation.explanation: A semicolon links two closely related independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Identify the correctly punctuated sentence containing an introductory clause:

options.A: Although the storm was intense, the rescue team reached the stranded villagers.
options.B: Although the storm was intense the rescue team reached the stranded villagers.
options.C: Although, the storm was intense the rescue team reached.
options.D: Although the storm was intense; the rescue team reached.

Punctuation.explanation: An introductory dependent clause is separated from the main independent clause by a comma.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Which sentence correctly punctuates direct speech with a split quotation?

options.A: "I believe," murmured the doctor, "that the patient will recover soon."
options.B: "I believe", murmured the doctor "that the patient will recover soon".
options.C: "I believe" murmured the doctor, "that the patient will recover soon."
options.D: "I believe," murmured the doctor "that the patient will recover soon".

Punctuation.explanation: The first quote ends with a comma inside quotes, followed by the attribution tag, a comma, and the resumed quote.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Choose the sentence with correct hyphenation:

options.A: She is a well-known Pakistani biochemist.
options.B: She is a well known Pakistani biochemist.
options.C: She is a well; known Pakistani biochemist.
options.D: She is a well, known Pakistani biochemist.

Punctuation.explanation: Compound adjectives before a noun (well-known biochemist) take a hyphen.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Identify the correct use of the colon:

options.A: The syllabus comprises three subjects: Physics, Chemistry, and Biology.
options.B: The syllabus comprises: three subjects Physics, Chemistry, and Biology.
options.C: The syllabus: comprises three subjects Physics, Chemistry, and Biology.
options.D: The syllabus comprises three subjects; Physics, Chemistry, and Biology.

Punctuation.explanation: A colon introduces a formal list after an independent introductory statement.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Select the sentence with correct capitalization:

options.A: The Prime Minister addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
options.B: The prime minister addressed the United nations general assembly in New York.
options.C: The Prime minister addressed the united nations General Assembly in New york.
options.D: The Prime Minister Addressed The United Nations General Assembly In New York.

Punctuation.explanation: Official titles, proper organization names, and place names must be capitalized.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Choose the sentence that correctly distinguishes "its" from "it's":

options.A: The bird flapped its wings because it's learning to fly.
options.B: The bird flapped it's wings because its learning to fly.
options.C: The bird flapped its' wings because it's learning to fly.
options.D: The bird flapped its wings because its learning to fly.

Punctuation.explanation: "Its" is possessive (its wings); "it's" is the contraction of "it is" (it's learning).

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Identify the sentence with correct punctuation of non-defining relative clause:

options.A: Quaid-e-Azam, who founded Pakistan, was a visionary leader.
options.B: Quaid-e-Azam who founded Pakistan was a visionary leader.
options.C: Quaid-e-Azam, who founded Pakistan was a visionary leader.
options.D: Quaid-e-Azam who founded Pakistan, was a visionary leader.

Punctuation.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses provide parenthetical information and must be enclosed in commas.

Punctuation.subject: English
Punctuation.question: Select the correctly punctuated exclamatory sentence:

options.A: What a picturesque valley Swat is!
options.B: What a picturesque valley Swat is?
options.C: What a picturesque valley Swat is.
options.D: What a picturesque valley, Swat is.

Punctuation.explanation: Exclamatory sentences expressing deep appreciation or surprise end with an exclamation mark (!).

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: Choose the modal expressing strong moral obligation: "We ______ respect our parents."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Ought to" conveys moral duty and obligation.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "You ______ not smoke inside the hospital premises."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Must not" expresses strict prohibition and legal enforcement.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "______ I borrow your pen for a moment?"
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "May" is standard for formal polite requests.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "He ______ swim across the river when he was young."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Could" expresses general past ability.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "It ______ rain later today, so take an umbrella."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Might" expresses a possibility.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "You ______ not worry about the arrangements; I will handle them."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Need not" expresses absence of obligation.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "If you worked harder, you ______ pass the examination."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: Second conditional main clause requires modal auxiliary "would".

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "He ______ have reached Karachi by now."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Must have + V3" expresses logical deduction/certainty about past event.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "She ______ play the piano exceptionally well."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Can" denotes present acquired ability/talent.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "______ you please pass the water pitcher?"
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Could" is standard for polite requests.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "We ______ to help the flood victims."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: Only "ought" is followed by the to-infinitive ("ought to").

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "Candidates ______ answer all five questions."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Shall" in regulatory/official contexts denotes formal command/requirement.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "How ______ you speak to me like that!"
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Dare" as semi-modal expresses indignation/courage to do something.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "He ______ used to wake up at 5 AM daily."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Used to" functions directly as the semi-modal expressing past habit.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "You ______ see a doctor immediately."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Should" gives advice and recommendation.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "______ God bless you with good health!"
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "May" introduces optative blessings.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "He said he ______ come if invited."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: Past sequence of tense converts "will" to "would".

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "You ______ leave early today if you finish your work."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "May" grants formal permission.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "I ______ rather starve than beg."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Would rather" expresses preference.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "She ______ have forgotten the appointment."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Might have + V3" expresses past possibility.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "______ I carry your luggage for you?"
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Shall I...?" offers assistance in polite formal speech.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "You ______ not pay for this; it is free of cost."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Need not" signifies lack of necessity.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "He ______ be at home right now because his car is outside."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Must" indicates strong logical deduction based on evidence.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "She ______ speak four languages fluently."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Can" denotes present linguistic ability.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "Drivers ______ wear seatbelts at all times."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Must" denotes legal obligation.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "______ you like a cup of green tea?"
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Would you like...?" is standard for polite hospitality offers.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "He told me that he ______ solve that difficult question."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: Past indirect speech converts "can" to "could".

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "You ______ better consult a specialist."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: The fixed idiom for strong advice is "had better + base verb".

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "We ______ obey the traffic signals."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: Legal compliance requires "must".

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "He ______ to study late into the night."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Used" pairs with "to" to denote past habit.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "______ you mind closing the window?"
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Would you mind + V-ing" expresses polite request.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "The sky is overcast; it ______ rain any minute."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "May" expresses factual likelihood.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "We ______ not tell lies."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Should not" expresses ethical recommendation.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "He ______ have taken my notebook by mistake."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Could have + V3" indicates past possibility.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "No citizen ______ violate the constitution."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: Legal statutes use "shall" to express mandatory prohibition.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "______ you please lend me your calculator?"
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Will you please...?" makes a polite request.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "She ______ to have known better."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Ought" requires "to have + V3".

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "You ______ not drive without a valid driving license."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: Strict legal prohibition takes "must not".

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "I ______ do my best to win the championship."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Will" with first-person pronoun expresses strong determination.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: "Which auxiliary is a pure modal verb?"
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Must" has only modal functions without primary verb forms.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: Which modal verb expresses moral obligation or duty?
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Ought to" expresses moral duty, social responsibility, or ethical advisability.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: Choose the appropriate modal for logical deduction/certainty: "The lights are off; they ________ be sleeping."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Must" expresses strong logical deduction or certainty based on available evidence.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: Fill in the blank for polite permission: "________ I have the honor of introducing our chief guest?"
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "May" is the standard formal modal for asking polite permission.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: Identify the semi-modal verb in English:
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Need", "dare", and "used to" are classified as semi-modals (marginal auxiliaries).

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: Fill in the blank expressing past unfulfilled ability: "He ________ the championship if he had practiced regularly."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Could have + V3" expresses ability in the past that was not realized.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: Choose the modal expressing strong prohibition: "You ________ disclose this classified information to anyone."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Must not" (mustn't) expresses strict prohibition or absolute prohibition by rule.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: Fill in the blank: "When I was in primary school, I ________ swim across the canal."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Could" expresses general ability in the past.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: Identify the sentence where "used to" expresses a discontinued past habit:

options.A: My grandfather used to take a morning walk by the river.
options.B: This tool is used to tighten screws.
options.C: He is used to working under pressure.
options.D: Wood is used to manufacture paper.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Used to + V1" describes a habitual action or state in the past that no longer occurs.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: Choose the modal indicating advisability or mild recommendation:

options.A: You should consult a physician before starting this rigorous regimen.
options.B: You must consult a physician immediately by law.
options.C: You can consult a physician if you wish.
options.D: You might consult a physician if forced.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Should" gives advice, suggestions, or mild recommendations.

Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.subject: English
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.question: Fill in the blank: "You ________ submit the draft today; tomorrow is the deadline."
Modals/Auxiliary Verbs.explanation: "Need not" indicates absence of obligation or necessity.

Clauses.subject: English

Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses

Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the clause: "We will leave *as soon as the rain stops*."
Clauses.explanation: Modifies the verb "leave" by specifying the time condition.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the clause: "This is the town *where Allama Iqbal was born*."
Clauses.explanation: Modifies the noun "the town", functioning as an adjective clause.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the clause: "He worked so diligently *that he topped the board*."
Clauses.explanation: Introduced by "so...that" expressing result.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the clause: "Although *he was severely injured*, he completed the race."
Clauses.explanation: Introduced by "Although", expressing contrast or concession.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the clause: "*What he said* was completely true."
Clauses.explanation: Acts as the subject of the predicate verb "was".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the clause: "He ran fast *so that he might catch the train*."
Clauses.explanation: Introduced by "so that", indicating purpose.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the clause: "If *you respect others*, others will respect you."
Clauses.explanation: Introduced by "If", expressing condition.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the clause: "He did the work *as he was instructed*."
Clauses.explanation: Introduced by "as", describing how the work was done.

options.B: A clause that always begins with a subordinate conjunction
options.C: A clause that lacks a finite verb
options.D: A clause that modifies a noun only

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the clause: "I know the reason *why he was absent*."
Clauses.explanation: Modifies the noun "the reason", making it an adjective clause.

Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the clause: "I know *why he was absent*."
Clauses.explanation: Direct object of "know" without an antecedent noun, making it a noun clause.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the clause: "She is taller *than her sister is*."
Clauses.explanation: Expresses comparison of degree introduced by "than".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the clause: "*Whoever arrives first* will receive the prize."
Clauses.explanation: Functions as the subject of the sentence.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the clause: "He is looking for a house *which has a garden*."
Clauses.explanation: Qualifies the noun "house".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "Because *he was ill*, he stayed home."
Clauses.explanation: Introduced by "Because", giving the cause.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "You may sit *wherever you like*."
Clauses.explanation: Introduced by "wherever", specifying location.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "Tell me *where you live*."
Clauses.explanation: Direct object of the imperative verb "Tell".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "The building, *which was constructed in 1900*, was renovated."
Clauses.explanation: Enclosed by commas providing supplementary descriptive info.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "No one knows *how the accident happened*."
Clauses.explanation: Object of transitive verb "knows".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "The news *that he won the gold medal* delighted his parents."
Clauses.explanation: In apposition to the abstract noun "The news".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "He worked hard *lest he should fail*."
Clauses.explanation: Introduced by "lest", expressing negative purpose.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "I will call you *when I reach home*."
Clauses.explanation: Specifies the time of the main action.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "The watch *that my father gave me* is waterproof."
Clauses.explanation: Modifies the noun "watch".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "Pay attention to *what the teacher explains*."

options.A: Noun clause as object of preposition

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "He speaks *as though he knew everything*."
Clauses.explanation: Introduced by "as though", expressing hypothetical manner.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "Unless *you tell the truth*, you will be punished."
Clauses.explanation: Introduced by "Unless", setting the condition.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "We returned *after the sun had set*."
Clauses.explanation: Time clause introduced by "after".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "He is the gentleman *whose car was damaged*."
Clauses.explanation: Modifies "gentleman" using relative possessive "whose".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "It seems *that it will rain today*."
Clauses.explanation: Completes the predicate following linking verb "seems".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "*Since you are tired*, take some rest."
Clauses.explanation: "Since" functions here as a causal conjunction.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "The student *whom the principal praised* stood first."
Clauses.explanation: Modifies "The student".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "He will go *wherever duty calls him*."
Clauses.explanation: Locational subordinate clause.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "He is as strong *as an ox is*."
Clauses.explanation: Compares degree of physical strength.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "My belief is *that hard work always pays*."
Clauses.explanation: Predicate noun clause renaming the subject "My belief".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "Though *he was exhausted*, he continued studying."
Clauses.explanation: Expresses contrast with "Though".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "She was weeping *because she had lost her purse*."
Clauses.explanation: Gives the underlying reason.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "A clause must contain:"

options.A: A subject and a finite predicate verb

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify: "The fact *that he is innocent* has been proven."

options.A: Noun clause in apposition to "The fact"

Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the underlined clause: "What he proposed during the meeting was accepted by all."

Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: In "The student who secured the first position was awarded a gold medal," what type of clause is "who secured the first position"?
Clauses.explanation: It modifies the noun "student" and restricts/defines its identity without commas, making it a defining relative clause.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the adverb clause of concession in the sentence: "Though he was exhausted, he completed the marathon."
Clauses.explanation: "Though he was exhausted" expresses concession/contrast and modifies the main verb phrase.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: In "She promised that she would return before sunset," the clause "that she would return before sunset" is a/an:

options.A: Noun clause functioning as object of the transitive verb

Clauses.explanation: It answers "what did she promise?", functioning as the direct object of "promised".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the adverb clause of reason: "The match was called off because the pitch was waterlogged."
Clauses.explanation: "Because the pitch was waterlogged" answers why the match was called off, acting as an adverb clause of reason.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: In "The house where the poet lived has been converted into a museum," the clause "where the poet lived" is a/an:
Clauses.explanation: It qualifies and describes the noun "house", making it an adjective (relative) clause introduced by relative adverb "where".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the adverb clause of purpose: "We eat so that we may live."
Clauses.explanation: "So that we may live" expresses the purpose of eating, introduced by the conjunction of purpose "so that".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: In "I will phone you as soon as I reach the station," the clause "as soon as I reach the station" is an:
Clauses.explanation: "As soon as I reach the station" denotes the temporal point when the phone call will occur.

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Identify the noun clause functioning as the object of a preposition: "Pay close attention to what the instructor explains."
Clauses.explanation: "What the instructor explains" acts as the object of the preposition "to".

Clauses.subject: English
Clauses.topic: Independent, Noun, Adjective, and Adverbial clauses
Clauses.question: Which sentence contains a non-defining relative clause?

options.A: Lahore, which is known for its historic gardens, attracts tourists worldwide.
options.B: The city which is known for historic gardens attracts tourists.
options.C: The tourists visited the city that has historic gardens.
options.D: The garden where the tourists met was scenic.

Clauses.explanation: Enclosed by commas, "which is known for its historic gardens" provides additional, non-essential parenthetical detail.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Positive degree of "worst" is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: The base positive form is "bad" (bad - worse - worst).

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Superlative degree of "far" (distance) is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: For physical distance, "farthest" is the standard superlative.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: "No other metal is as heavy as lead." Change to Superlative:

options.A: Lead is the heaviest of all metals.
options.B: Lead is heavier than most metals.
options.D: No metal is heavier than lead.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Converts positive comparison into superlative statement.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: "Lahore is larger than most cities in Pakistan." Change to Positive:

options.A: Very few cities in Pakistan are as large as Lahore.
options.B: No other city in Pakistan is as large as Lahore.
options.C: Lahore is a large city in Pakistan.
options.D: Lahore is the largest city in Pakistan.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Larger than most" converts to "Very few...are as large as".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Comparative degree of "little" (amount) is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: The comparative form of "little" is "less".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Superlative degree of "beautiful" is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Multi-syllabic adjectives form superlative with "most".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Which adjective CANNOT be compared (absolute adjective)?
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Unique" represents an absolute quality that cannot logically be graded.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: "Mount Everest is the highest peak in the world." Change to Comparative:

options.A: Mount Everest is higher than all other peaks in the world.
options.B: Mount Everest is higher than any peaks.
options.C: Mount Everest is very high peak.
options.D: No peak is higher than Mount Everest.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Superlative converts to "higher than all other peaks".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Comparative degree of "elder" indicates:

options.A: Seniority in age among family members

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Elder" is used exclusively for family relations.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Choose the correct sentence:

options.A: He is the senior of the two candidates.
options.B: He is the most senior of the two candidates.
options.C: He is senior than the two candidates.
options.D: He is more senior of the two.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: When comparing exactly two items, comparative with "the" is used ("the senior of the two").

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Comparative degree of "good" is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Irregular gradation: good - better - best.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Superlative degree of "late" (time):
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Latest" refers to the most recent time; "last" refers to order/position.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: "Latter" refers to:

options.A: The second of two things mentioned

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Latter" denotes the second item in a pair.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: "He is ______ than his brother."
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Comparison between two items uses comparative "-er".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: "She is the ______ girl in the school."
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Comparison among three or more items uses superlative "most intelligent".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Positive degree of "least" is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Gradation: little - less - least.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Which adjective is absolute and has no comparative degree?
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Dead" is an absolute state.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Select the correct comparative form:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Four-syllable adjectives form comparative using "more".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: "Gold is heavier than silver." Change to Positive:

options.A: Silver is not as heavy as gold.
options.B: Silver is as heavy as gold.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Affirmative comparative converts to negative positive ("not as heavy as").

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Which of the following is correct?

options.A: This room is more spacious than that one.
options.B: This room is spaciouser than that one.
options.C: This room is most spacious than that one.
options.D: This room is more spacious that one.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Spacious" takes "more" for comparative.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Comparative of "many" / "much" is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Gradation: many/much - more - most.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: "Of the three brothers, Ali is the ______."
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Comparison among three entities requires the superlative degree.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Comparative of "dry" is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Consonant + y changes to -ier (drier).

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Superlative of "narrow" is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Two-syllable adjectives ending in -ow take -est (narrowest).

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: "He is as wise as Solomon." Change to Comparative:

options.A: Solomon was not wiser than him (he is).

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Positive equality statement converts to negative comparative.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Select the correct double comparative sentence:

options.A: The higher you climb, the colder it gets.
options.B: Higher you climb, colder it gets.
options.C: The more high you climb, the more cold it gets.
options.D: The highest you climb, the coldest it gets.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Double parallel comparison formula: "The + comparative..., the + comparative...".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Comparative form of "friendly" is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Friendlier" or "more friendly" are standard comparative forms.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Which adjective has no degrees of comparison?
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Geometric shapes (circular, square, triangular) are absolute adjectives.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: "This is the ______ moment of my life."
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: y preceded by consonant changes to -iest (happiest).

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Comparative of "near" indicating order is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Next" indicates ordinal sequence; "nearest" indicates physical distance.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: "Iron is more useful than any other metal." Change to Superlative:

options.A: Iron is the most useful of all metals.
options.C: Iron is useful than all metals.
options.D: All metals are useful like iron.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Standard superlative transformation.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Comparative of "old" for general age is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Older" is used for persons or things generally, followed by "than".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Comparative degree of "clever" is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Cleverer" is the standard comparative form.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: "Shakespeare is greater than all other English poets." Change to Positive:

options.A: No other English poet is as great as Shakespeare.
options.B: All English poets are as great as Shakespeare.
options.D: Very few English poets are great.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Comparative with "all other" converts to "No other...is as great as".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Select the correct sentence with "preferable":

options.B: Health is more preferable than wealth.
options.D: Health is most preferable to wealth.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Preferable" has comparative sense already and takes "to", never "more" or "than".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Superlative of "badly" is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Adverb "badly" shares comparative "worse" and superlative "worst".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Superlative of "fore" (position):
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Foremost" or "first" is the superlative of fore.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: "Very few cricketers are as famous as Babar Azam." Change to Superlative:

options.A: Babar Azam is one of the most famous cricketers.
options.B: Babar Azam is the most famous cricketer.
options.D: No cricketer is more famous than Babar Azam.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Very few...as famous as" converts to "one of the most famous".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Which adjective cannot be paired with "more"?
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Perfect" is an absolute adjective that cannot logically be graded.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Comparative of "polite" is:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Both "politer" and "more polite" are standard.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Convert into comparative degree: "Iron is the most useful of all metals."

options.A: Iron is more useful than any other metal.
options.B: Iron is useful than all metals.
options.C: No other metal is more useful than iron.
options.D: Iron is most useful than any metal.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Superlative "the most useful of all metals" converts to comparative using "more useful than any other metal".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Convert into positive degree: "The pen is mightier than the sword."

options.A: The sword is not as mighty as the pen.
options.B: The sword is mighty as the pen.
options.C: No sword is mightier than the pen.
options.D: The pen is as mighty as the sword.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Comparative "A is mightier than B" transforms to negative positive "B is not as/so mighty as A".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Identify the correct superlative form of "far" referring to distance:
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Farthest" refers specifically to physical distance, while "furthest" can also mean figurative depth or degree.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Choose the correct sentence comparing two family members with comparative degree:

options.A: He is the elder of the two brothers.
options.B: He is the eldest of the two brothers.
options.C: He is elder than the two brothers.
options.D: He is more elder of the two brothers.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: When comparing exactly two members of a family, the comparative with "the" ("the elder") is used.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Identify the irregular comparative and superlative forms of "bad":
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: The irregular degrees of "bad" are: bad (positive), worse (comparative), worst (superlative).

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Choose the grammatically sound comparative structure:

options.A: The climate of Multan is hotter than that of Murree.
options.B: The climate of Multan is hotter than Murree.
options.C: The climate of Multan is more hotter than Murree.
options.D: The climate of Multan is hot than Murree.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: To avoid illogical comparison of climate to a city, use "than that of Murree".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Transform to superlative: "No other student in the class is as diligent as Hamza."

options.A: Hamza is the most diligent student in the class.
options.B: Hamza is more diligent than any student.
options.C: Hamza is the diligentest student in the class.
options.D: Hamza is most diligent than all students.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "No other... as diligent as Hamza" converts directly to "Hamza is the most diligent student in the class".

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Fill in the blank: "This is the ________ edition of the encyclopedia."
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: "Latest" refers to the most recent time or publication, whereas "last" means final in a series.

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Select the grammatically accurate sentence when choosing between two alternatives:

options.A: Of the two proposals, this one is the better.
options.B: Of the two proposals, this one is the best.
options.C: Of the two proposals, this one is more better.
options.D: Of the two proposals, this one is gooder.

Degrees of Comparison.explanation: For a choice between two alternatives, use the comparative degree with "the" ("the better").

Degrees of Comparison.subject: English
Degrees of Comparison.question: Which adjective does NOT admit degrees of comparison because it is absolute?
Degrees of Comparison.explanation: Absolute adjectives like "unique", "perfect", "dead", and "square" cannot logically be compared.

Vocabulary & Comprehension.topic: Synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitutions, context clues
Vocabulary & Comprehension.question: What is the antonym of "artificial"?
Vocabulary & Comprehension.explanation: "Artificial" means human-made; its antonym is "natural".

Vocabulary & Comprehension.explanation: Panacea is a universal remedy.

Vocabulary & Comprehension.question: What is the synonym of "diligent"?
Vocabulary & Comprehension.explanation: "Diligent" means showing care and conscientiousness in work.

Vocabulary & Comprehension.question: What is the synonym of "perilous"?

Vocabulary & Comprehension.subject: English
Vocabulary & Comprehension.topic: Synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitutions, context clues
Vocabulary & Comprehension.question: A person who looks at the bright side of things is an:
Vocabulary & Comprehension.explanation: An optimist holds a hopeful outlook.

Vocabulary & Comprehension.subject: English

Vocabulary & Comprehension.question: What is the synonym of "tranquil"?
Vocabulary & Comprehension.explanation: "Tranquil" means calm and free from disturbance.

Vocabulary & Comprehension.subject: English
Vocabulary & Comprehension.topic: Synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitutions, context clues
Vocabulary & Comprehension.question: What is the antonym of "valiant"?
Vocabulary & Comprehension.explanation: "Valiant" means showing courage; antonym is "cowardly".

Vocabulary & Comprehension.question: The first public performance or speech of someone is called a:

Vocabulary & Comprehension.question: What is the synonym of "augment"?

Vocabulary & Comprehension.question: Murder of a king is termed:

Vocabulary & Comprehension.topic: Synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitutions, context clues
Vocabulary & Comprehension.question: What is the antonym of "arrogant"?
